title: Transferable genetic toolsets for nonmodel gut Clostridia enable in vivo reversible control of metabolite production - Nature Biotechnology
text:
AbstractGut Clostridia species, including commensal members of the Clostridiaceae and Lachnospiraceae families, maintain microbiota homeostasis and influence human health and disease; however, adequate genetic toolsets to study abundant but nonmodel gut Clostridia are lacking. Here we present a set of transferable and modular genetic toolsets that function broadly across phylogenetically diverse gut Clostridia. We first identify a panel of strong constitutive promoters that drive robust gene expression across diverse clostridial strains. We then develop an inducible promoter system that enables precise, tunable gene regulation and facilitates the implementation of CRISPR–Cas gene-deletion systems. We apply this system for targeted and reversible control of trimethylamine and deoxycholic acid production, two microbiota-derived metabolites implicated in host lipid metabolism and diseases, in mice. This robust genetic toolkit for nonmodel gut Clostridia enables functional studies to causally link microbiota genes to host physiology and disease, paving the way for therapeutic genetic engineering of microbiota.

Additional informationPublisher’s note Springer Nature remains neutral with regard to jurisdictional claims in published maps and institutional affiliations.Extended dataExtended Data Fig. 1 Promoter activity screen in C. sporogenes ATCC15579.a. A total of 29 promoters (Table S2), including previously reported strong promoters (Pfdx and Pthl), metatranscriptome-identified candidates, and additional promoters, were tested for their ability to drive nanoluc expression in C. sporogenes ATCC15579. Promoter strength was quantified by luminescence-based reporter assay, with relative luminescence values plotted on a logarithmic scale. Promoters are color-coded according to predicted functional categories, as in Fig. 1b, c. NC, promoterless negative control. Promoter numbers highlighted in green indicate candidates identified through metatranscriptomics-based screening (Table S5). Data in (a) are presented as mean ± SEM from two or three biological replicates. b. Representative scatter plot showing the correlation between promoter activities measured in C. sporogenes ATCC15579 and E. bolteae ATCC BAA-613. Luminescence signals from the promoter screen were quantified in both species, normalized as fold change relative to the negative control, and subsequently Z-transformed (mean = 0, SD = 1). Associations were assessed using the Pearson correlation coefficient, with the corresponding r and p values indicated on the plot. A two-sided significance threshold of α = 0.05 was used. In addition, a linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept was fitted to account for potential promoter-specific variability, and the fitted regression line is shown. Correlations with |r| ≥ 0.2 were considered moderate.Source dataExtended Data Fig. 2 In vitro comparison of full-length and shortened promoter activities in E. bolteae ATCC BAA-613.The strengths of four full-length promoters (P2, P4, P5, P6) were compared to their shortened versions (PS1 or PS2), which retain the predicted −10/−35 motifs. Most truncated promoters exhibited similar strength to their full-length counterparts. Promoter activity was quantified using a luminescence-based assay, and relative fold changes were normalized to the promoterless negative control (NC). Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. from three biological replicates (n = 3). For the left and right panels, statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test, using the original promoters as the control group. For the middle two panels, statistical significance was determined by an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test. Only statistically significant differences are indicated with exact P values.Source dataExtended Data Fig. 3 Optimization of inducible promoter systems in non-model Clostridia by tuning tetR expression.a.
